name: Water loading / hydration maxxing

card.summary: Drinking large amounts of water for skin and depuffing: fixed targets like eight glasses lack scientific basis, and excess carries hyponatremia risk.
card.note: Excessive water intake can cause hyponatremia.

quick.overview:
Water loading, or hydration maxxing, is drinking large volumes of water in pursuit of clearer skin and less facial puffiness. It is a common wellness and looksmaxxing habit.

Wikipedia describes the 'eight glasses a day' advice as unscientific and says thirst is a better guide than a fixed amount. The sources reviewed do not discuss skin hydration effects.
quick.mechanism: Believers say hydration plumps skin and flushes retained water. The sources reviewed do not cover a skin mechanism.
quick.risks: Drinking too much water too quickly causes hyponatremia, which Wikipedia says can cause death in minutes or hours.

lead: Water loading, sometimes called hydration maxxing, is the practice of deliberately drinking large quantities of water, with the aim of plumper, clearer-looking skin and less facial puffiness. It is one of the most common wellness habits in appearance communities because it is free, easy and tied to a widely held belief that well-hydrated skin looks better.

Guideline figures give a sense of ordinary intake. The US Adequate Intake for total water, counting water from food, is 4.0 L a day for men and 3.0 L for women, while the European Food Safety Authority recommends 2.5 L for men and 2.0 L for women; about 80 percent of total intake comes from drink [1]. Wikipedia describes the "eight glasses a day" rule as not scientifically based and says thirst is a better guide [1].

Two small studies have looked at water intake and skin. A 2015 study of 49 healthy women reported that about 2 L of extra water a day for a month changed superficial and deep skin hydration, mostly in women who habitually drank less [3]. A 2024 study of 43 women found that moisturizer use had a more favourable effect on skin hydration than extra water [4]. Drinking far more than the body needs can cause water intoxication and hyponatremia, a potentially fatal drop in blood sodium [1][2].

chain: Better skin hydration (reported in people who drink little)
Plumper, healthier-looking skin; less perceived puffiness
angle.text: People drink extra water hoping for a more hydrated complexion and a less bloated face. Studies report a skin-hydration change in people who start from low intake, while the face-depuffing claim has not been tested directly.

paras: Needs vary with activity, age, health and environment, and about 80 percent of total water intake comes from drink, with the remainder from food [1]. Wikipedia notes that the common eight-glasses advice lacks a scientific basis and that thirst is a better guide than a fixed amount [1].

In a 2015 study in Clinical, Cosmetic and Investigational Dermatology, Palma and colleagues grouped 49 healthy women by habitual intake, with the cut-off at 3,200 mL a day. Roughly 2 L of additional water daily for one month significantly changed superficial and deep skin hydration, especially in the lower-intake group, and biomechanical measures shifted similarly. The authors concluded that higher dietary water may positively affect skin physiology, particularly in people who drink little [3].

In a 2024 Annals of Dermatology study of 43 healthy women, people who drank more than 1 L daily were compared with those who drank less. Some forearm, hand and shin sites in groups receiving added water or moisturizer showed higher skin hydration at week 4 than at baseline, and moisturizer had the more favourable effect [4].

A 2023 cross-sectional study of acne patients in Karachi found that lower daily water intake (fewer than eight glasses) was significantly associated with acne, alongside oily and sugary foods [5]. No studies were found on high water intake and facial puffiness.

Water intoxication is a potentially fatal disturbance of brain function that occurs when excess water intake pushes electrolytes out of safe limits. Wikipedia lists water-drinking contests and prolonged exercise with heavy fluid intake as causes behind most deaths in healthy people; early symptoms include headache, confusion and irritability, and severe cases cause brain swelling, seizures, coma and death [2].

Healthy kidneys can excrete roughly 800 mL to 1 L of water per hour, and drinking six litres in three hours has caused a death [2]. Documented cases include a 2007 radio contest in which a woman died after drinking nearly 2 US gallons [2].
